newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND PLEDGES CRACKDOWN ON DRUGS.
newsitem.headline: POLAND PLEDGES CRACKDOWN ON DRUGS.

text.p: The Polish police declared war against drug dealers and smugglers on Tuesday to cut major international drug trafficking routes and prevent the country from becoming a narcotics consumer market.
"Drug abuses and crime related to them are rising steeply..., we must take tough measures against that," the recently appointed police chief, Marek Papala, told a news conference.

He said international drug cartels were using Poland as a transit country for smuggling drugs to Western Europe and the United States from South America, Asia and Africa while dealers were begining to penetrate schools and universities.
"The situation is getting beyond the level of the society's tolerance," he said.

Papala said he had decided to create a special anti-narcotics bureau within the police to coordinate efforts of other state institutions, such as the security police and the border guard to fight drug-related crime.
The bureau will closely cooperate with Interpol and police in Western countries and will widely use operational techniques such as "sting" actions, telephone tapping and undercover agents, he said.

Papala pledged the buraeu, initially employing 400 officers now dispersed throughout various police units, would not lack funds despite the Polish police's meager budget. "The money for this purpose must be found and will be found," he said.
He also said that one of the bureau's priorities would be to liquidate laboratories manufacturing amphetamine, of which Poland is Europe's major supplier.

"Some of these facilities are really factories and not laboratories..., which employ high-class chemistry experts," he said, adding that Polish amphetamine was popular in the West because it was pure.

Poland has seen a steep rise in drug consumption and trafficking after the fall of communism in 1989 when it libaralised travel regualtions and curbed powers of the police, often abused under the old system.

The number of officially registered drug addicts increased to nearly 20,000 last year from about 14,000 in 1990 as new narcotics -- heroin, cocaine, amphetamine, marijuana and LSD -- began to replace the contaminated, home-made poppy-seed extract, known as "kompot."
Last year, the police and border guard detected 97 cases of cross-border drug smuggling, 28 more than in 1995.
"But all this is just a tip of an iceberg," Papala said.
